Richard Sterban, longtime Oak Ridge Boys bass singer, dies at 83
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Richard Sterban, the longtime bass singer for the Oak Ridge Boys whose deep voice became a signature of the group’s hit “Elvira,” has died. He was 83.
The Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum lists Sterban’s date of death as Nov. 14, 2026. A cause of death was not included in the museum’s announcement.
“It is with heavy hearts that we announce the passing of our partner and brother, Richard Sterban,” the Oak Ridge Boys said in a statement on social media.
A voice behind the Oak Ridge Boys’ hits
Born in Camden, New Jersey, on April 24, 1943, Sterban sang with J.D. Sumner and the Stamps, a gospel group that performed with Elvis Presley, before joining the Oak Ridge Boys in 1972, according to the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum.
The Oak Ridge Boys’ 1981 hit “Elvira,” featuring Sterban’s bass vocals, reached No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on the pop chart, according to the museum. The group was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015.
“Richard Sterban was a musical bridge builder,” museum CEO Kyle Young said in a statement. “He used his unmistakable bass voice to connect commercial country music to its deep gospel roots.”

Card collectors and families gather at Central Maine Card Extravaganza
text:
FAIRFIELD, Maine — Collectors gathered Sunday at the Fairfield Community Center for the Central Maine Card Extravaganza, where about 50 vendors offered sports cards, Pokémon cards, memorabilia and more.
The event has been held for about three years, with two shows each year, according to promoter Michael Huard. He said attendees of all ages come to browse, buy and trade.
“A lot of younger guys, you’ll see them walking around with their little briefcases, and they’ll go up to the tables and try to make deals and trade,” Huard said.
Among sports cards, memorabilia, and popular franchises, many collectors say they got into the hobby at an early age. For baseball card collector Joshua Hart, he got his start at eight years old.
“Me and my father started years ago building sets, the 1956 top sets. And from there I always found a love for it and just continued to do it,” said Hart.
Participants said that it’s just an event for diehard collectors -- It’s a chance for families to enjoy the hobby together.
“I think it brings everyone together in a sense that we’re all after one certain thing,” said Pokémon card collector Nakoa Parsons, “Generally speaking, we’re in a good space. At least up here in Maine, it’s been a very healthy community.”
“I’ve never seen so many dads with their kids going out and looking at their stuff It’s kind of neat,” said Huard.
Huard encourages anyone interested in the hobby to start by collecting what they like
“Just go out and get some cards and get started and hit some shows, and I think you’ll be able to be part of the community and the collecting pretty easily,” said Huard.

What to know as US air travel continues to recover from Friday’s nationwide ground stop
text:
(AP) - U.S. air travel is recovering smoothly after a nationwide ground stop, though some passengers are both weary and wary after repeated flight delays and cancelations.
Just over 1,300 of the more than 26,000 flights scheduled for Sunday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. That amounts to about 5.2% of scheduled flights. Prior to Friday’s ground stop, the average cancellation rate for U.S. departures was 3.4%.
The four-hour stoppage was the longest in 25 years. It caused massive travel disruptions, but officials said they expected airline schedules to fully recover by late Sunday or early Monday.
“As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday. “We’re well on our way.”
At Nashville International Airport, Lona Ivers, Will Ahern and their children were trying to get home to Minnesota after vacationing in Tennessee. They made it from Knoxville to Nashville with no problems Saturday, only to have their flight to Minnesota canceled.
“We thought we were safe, but we weren’t,” Ivers said.
Instead, they spent the night in a hotel and were re-booked on a flight not scheduled to leave Nashville until late Sunday night.
“I already hate flying so this just makes me hate it more,” said 14-year-old Bella Ahern. “Everything about this sucks. I already hated airports, and now I’m stuck here.”
Here’s what to know:
Flights have resumed but disruption continues
In New Jersey, Ashley Lynn Qua said she arrived at Newark Liberty International Airport three hours early for her Sunday flight with all her essentials in her carry-on and armed with “an extra ounce of kindness.”
“I’m not blaming anybody like the pilots, the flight attendants, the guy who’s serving me my third coffee of the morning. Those are not the people I’m upset with,” she said. “As I interact with everybody at the airport today, I know it’s not their fault.”
Qua, 32, a clean energy researcher, was on her way to a conference in Las Vegas. While her flight was expected to be on time, some of her colleagues were dealing with delays and cancellations.
Pete Alfieris, 60, was hoping to return home to Florida after attending a wedding in New York.
“Our flight has been delayed an hour or so so far, so fingers crossed that we can get out of here and go back to sun in Florida,” he said. “It’s just too cold up here.”
Alfieris, a facilities manager, said the entire travel system should be revamped.
“Honestly, it’s very perplexing,” he said. “We are in 2026, 2027. You know, we should have better infrastructure.”
Officials point to 2 potential problem sites
The Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday described a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as potential sources for the problem, which involved excess data flooding the air traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds.
Duffy said after a contractor replaced old copper wire with new fiber wire at the Arkansas site and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up in Texas, cascading into the ground stop.
“We didn’t think that should or would happen,” he told ABC’s “This Week.”
In multiple appearances on Sunday news shows, Duffy continued to press Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air traffic control infrastructure.
“I can’t apologize for what was passed on to us. And I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats, because it’s all of them. It goes back, 20, 25, 30 years of a lack of investment,” he told NBC’s “Meet the Press.”
The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. About 70% of copper wire has been switched to fiber already, officials said Saturday.
Stoppage was not related to any cyberattack or Microsoft outage
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack and no lives were at risk.
Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after its own massive outage. There was no indication the FAA ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Microsoft services offline Thursday, according to federal officials and a company spokesperson.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Users reported Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were interrupted.

BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The William S. Cohen school was transformed into a speedway Sunday morning as the Girl Scouts of Maine hosted an extra special event.

title: Giving Tuesday gift challenge could help 100s in northern Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A $50,000 gift match challenge to a local nonprofit by an anonymous donor for Giving Tuesday will make a huge difference for Mainers living with disabilities, said Living Innovations Community Resource Manager Angelina Jackman.
“We have a donor that has given us a gift challenge. If we can raise $50,000 as an organization on Giving Tuesday, he will match it,” she said. “That’s pretty huge. That’s astronomically huge.”
Falling on the day after Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday was created in 2012 for people to do generous acts for neighbors like painting and yard work or to donate labor or money to local nonprofits. For people with disabilities who are supported by Living Innovations, it makes a difference in daily survival, she said.
Worries about how to pay $7 for a bottle of medicated shampoo or new glasses broken during a seizure take the place of holiday primping, decorations and an ever-growing Santa gift list, she added.
“Giving Tuesday hits right around the holiday and many of our folks don’t have anyone to share or spend Christmas with,” she said. “And some of them wonder how they are going to pay for their heat instead of worrying about what they’re going to get for Christmas. We would love to raise $50,000. It would really impact hundreds of people’s lives.”
Living Innovations is a regional nonprofit and service organization supporting individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities across Maine, New Hampshire and Rhode Island. They support about 2,000 people — from children to people in their late 80s – in Maine alone.
Hundreds of people in the local community rely on Jackman and other staff for their day-to-day life, making sure they take their medications, go to doctor’s appointments, find jobs and in many ways live meaningful lives. As part of their work, staff help people live independently, teaching them the skills to do so.
But there are still times when they need extra support, such when the stove is a safety hazard and they have no means to cook, or they want to take a CPR class or buy non-slip shoes for work.
People take many things for granted, Jackman said.
For some of the people she works with, just getting to the store or a job is an extra challenge because they don’t have driver’s licenses or family in the area to help.
“When they come to us they don’t have a winter coat, or they want to get their first job, but they’ve never had a state ID, because they can’t afford it and they can’t drive all the way to Caribou to get one,” Jackman said.
This is where the Giving Tuesday match dollars will help, she said.
Jackman shared success stories of people Living Innovations supports, such as Patrick Duff-Hebert, who has been working for more than three years at the Northeastland Hotel in Presque Isle, and Noah Plavnik, who started his own successful Caribou-based house painting business, Big Moose Painting. She recalled people in their 50s who have never been to a movie theater and people staff have taught to hike, kayak and ride bikes.
Duff-Hebert said in a recent video that his job gives him the chance to get out into the community, connect with people and earn his own paycheck.
Then there is Caribou violinist Christiano Belzaire.
When Belzaire first went to Living Innovations, his work sheet said he could stock shelves. But what he really wanted was to play violin. The team got to work to make that possible.
“He never had a new violin to call his own. We worked with vocational rehab and the Mini Music Store, who donated half of the cost of the violin, to make sure he could afford it,” Jackman said.
Living Innovations can use donor funds for many reasons, but 100% of any funds raised goes to the people it supports, she said.
“We are very good stewards of the money that is given to us. We share back with our donors how the money has impacted us,” Jackman said. “You can see the work day after day. We invite our donors to come to our events and meet our individuals.”
To donate to Living Innovations on Giving Tuesday, visit their webpage. Jackman pointed to the $5 button on the site.
“That $5 could mean the difference between an individual having a shirt to land their first job, somebody getting a healthy meal or an oven mitt so they can take a pan out of the stove safely,” she said. “Whatever it is, all those little things we take for granted every day would help.”

text:
Thanksgiving’s Best Pie Isn’t Pumpkin or Apple. It’s a Maine Classic.
Thanksgiving is easily one of the greatest holidays of the year. It's right up there with Christmas, Easter, and, of course, the granddaddy of them all, Groundhog Day.
Seriously, what's not to love? It's a day dedicated to gathering with family and friends, consuming roughly 25,000 calories in a single sitting, and watching some questionable football between food-induced comas. Throw in a parade or two, an uncomfortable family conversation, too much wine. and a second helping of pie, and you've got yourself a perfect holiday.
It seems everyone has an opinion on what's the best part of a Thanksgiving meal. Is it the turkey? Perhaps the stuffing? How about that weird tube of cranberry sauce? However, everyone really knows it's the pie.
Nothing beats a slice (or two) of fresh, homemade pie on Thanksgiving. We may have no room for it in our stomachs, but that doesn't stop us from indulging.
My family is very lucky because they have a pretty great pie baker: me. Nothing makes me happier than spending a few hours of quality time in the kitchen, cranking out some delicious, homemade spherical gems.
What is the Best Pie for Thanksgiving?
Now, I'll make any pie that's requested, but there's one that truly reigns supreme. It's not apple, pumpkin, pecan, or even chocolate cream. As delicious as those all are, none of them compares to the absolute amazement that is Wild Maine Blueberry Pie.
I can already hear you saying, "Wait. This is ridiculous, Chris. Blueberry pie is for Easter and summertime."
Au contraire.
The blueberry is a perfectly acceptable fruit for all seasons. In fact, these delicious little things have become the stuff of legend for their incredible health benefits.
How Healthy are Maine Wild Blueberries?
According to verywellfit.com, blueberries are loaded with antioxidants to help improve brain function, fight inflammation, decrease cancer risk, and even potentially lower the risk of a heart attack.
And the wild Maine blueberry is even more impressive.
According to wildblueberries.com, these little wild Maine guys have up to twice as many antioxidants than cultivated blueberries.
Just think about that. You're practically eating health food while consuming them in a pie. (On a related note, I really hope my doctor doesn't read this.)
Also, the idea that blueberry pie only belongs in the warmer months is preposterous. Thanksgiving is loaded with fruit. There's that weird cranberry tube. Some folks include fruit in their stuffing. Citrus is often used to help brine or flavor turkey. Apples and pumpkins dominate the dessert table. I could keep going, but I think you get the point.
There's simply no logic behind limiting your blueberry intake just because some lame magazine or old tradition tells you it's not what the cool kids do.

Do yourself a favor and bake a Wild Maine Blueberry Pie this Thanksgiving. Your family will love it. And don't worry that blueberry season has passed. You can find frozen Maine blueberries in grocery stores across the country.

BAR HARBOR, Maine (WABI) - The Bar Harbor Historical Society is laying off its entire staff as it restructures this winter.
The board said the five current staff members have been let go as part of a business decision to “thoughtfully” reorganize while the La Rochelle Mansion Museum is closed for the season.

Officials say a tanker's steering failed before it crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans
text:
A tanker’s steering system failed and kept its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans, U.S. government safety officials said Sunday.
The preliminary finding from National Transportation Safety Board officials provided the first official word on what caused Friday’s crash of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker into the American Heritage cruise ship, which sent passengers, crew and two police officers plunging into the Mississippi River.
NTSB officials said during a briefing in New Orleans that it’s not yet clear what caused the steering failure.
“It could be many different things,” NTSB accident investigator Bart Barnum said. “That is something that we’re investigating very closely.”
The tanker, measuring about 520 feet (160 meters) long, had a crew of 19. The cruise ship, about 300 feet (91 meters) long, had 140 passengers and 50 crew onboard.
Officials said 32 people were taken to the hospital, including the two police officers who were thrown into the river when the boat rolled, but none of the injuries were critical. As of Sunday, six people remained hospitalized, the city of New Orleans said in a statement.
The tanker’s steering problem caused its rudder to remain in a starboard position, to the right, which sent the tanker veering toward the east bank of the river, where it hit the cruise ship two minutes after the rudder became stuck, Barnum said.
As the tanker approached the river’s east bank, the ship’s data recorder captured audio sounds “consistent” with the ship’s whistle going off, along with warnings and requests for assistance broadcast over the vessel’s marine radio, Barnum said. He added the data included commands to deploy the vessel anchors and emergency ship handling orders.
NTSB Member John DeLeeuw urged people with photos or video of the crash to submit them to his agency to help with its investigation, which is expected to result in a preliminary report within 30 days. He also praised the “the excellent response” from federal, state, local and private vessels that helped rescue people immediately after the crash.
The cruise ship capsized in 22 minutes, DeLeeuw said.
Just hours after the crash, the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans filed a federal lawsuit saying that the tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

title: Listen to the final song Dolly Parton ever recorded
text:
(Gray News) - You can now listen to the last song Dolly Parton recorded.
“Torn,” a duet between Parton and U2 lead singer Bono, was released Friday. It was the final track on the band’s 16th album, “Carnaval De Luz.”
The country song touches on “broken family ties,” according to Parton’s official website. She co-wrote the song with U2 and Irish singer-songwriter Johnny McDavid.
The song was recorded in Nashville in June, making it her final recorded vocal performance before her death.
“I hope you like what I did,” Parton said to Bono in a joint Instagram post in June when the duet was first announced. “Take from what it what you want and what you need, but I love the song, and I think it could be something really special. Thanks for including me in your life. I’ve always loved you and always will.”
In an interview with Rolling Stone, Bono said Parton “sang her heart out” when recording “Torn.” He also expressed how her death has impacted him regarding the song.
“When she was ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song. And you can hear that. And I can’t even listen to it now,” he said.
Parton died of cancer in August at the age of 80.

Follow these steps to identify birds quickly
text:
This story was originally published in February 2021.
The first point when it comes to identifying birds quickly is this: size matters. Color may catch the eye, but size is the first thing the brain registers. Perhaps that’s a throwback to our prehistoric ancestors, who had to make a quick judgment about whether a predator was big enough to eat them.
A particular bird species may have confusing color variations, depending on age and gender, but seldom does it vary in size. Young bald eagles go through several color plumages before reaching adulthood, but once they’re out of the nest, every eagle is eagle-sized. The first step in quickly identifying a bird is to judge its size.
Birds come in all sizes, from hummingbird to ostrich, but fortunately a lot of them can be grouped together by comparing them to common birds you already know. Your brain does it automatically. You can quickly judge if a bird is chickadee-size, robin-size, crow-size or larger. It’s often the first thing somebody says when they ask for help in identifying a bird: “It was yellow, about the size of a robin.”
A lot of birds can be grouped by size, but within each group, there is likely to be one that is much more common than all the others. It sort of becomes the default bird — the one you expect to see. When you see a bird in that size category, it’s natural that the next step is to determine whether it is your default bird, or not your default bird. For instance, sparrow identification is difficult. There are roughly 13 sparrow species that nest in Maine. But song sparrows are in every neighborhood following their arrival in April. Often, the first step in making a quick identification is to decide if a mystery sparrow is a song sparrow, or not a song sparrow.
In February, every hawk along Interstate 95 is a red-tailed hawk, unless it isn’t. On a summer mudflat, every shorebird is a semipalmated sandpiper, unless it isn’t. Every robin is a robin, unless it isn’t. Two robin-like birds from the West sometimes show up in Maine: Townsend’s solitaire and varied thrush. In January, an exceptionally rare redwing was discovered in a Portland flock of robins, only the second time this robin-like European species has ever been discovered in Maine. And the first step in identifying this thoroughly unexpected bird was to recognize that it wasn’t a robin.
Another tip: You are what you eat. The shape of every bird is largely determined by its diet. Wading birds have long legs, swimming birds have webbed feet, soaring birds have broad wings, etc. Bill shape is particularly determined by diet. The world is full of tiny, hard-to-identify birds. Often, a key step in figuring them out is to guess what they eat. Insect-eaters have thin bills, built for snatching bugs out of the air or gleaning them from under leaves. Seed-eaters have heavy bills, designed for cracking shells. The bigger the bill, the bigger the seed they can crack.
Probably the biggest secret is that color should always be treated with suspicion. Reds, blues and yellows may capture attention, but the colors are often unhelpful and even deceptive. A female scarlet tanager isn’t scarlet. A female redstart isn’t red. Scores of birds are yellow, and some species are virtually identical.
Birds have field marks, and any good guidebook takes pains to point them out. Fortunately, many of these marks fall into categories. About half of warblers have streaked breasts; half don’t. Same for sparrows. Roughly half of warblers have yellow throats. Half have wing bars. Noticing just one of these common field marks cuts the list of identification possibilities in half at a glance. Furthermore, a handful of birds have eye rings. Some have white outer tail feathers. Color can vary with age and gender, and change as birds molt into fall plumage, but most field marks remain fixed. It’s not hard to notice them. The trick is in remembering to look.

NEW YORK (AP) — Former NFL coach Rex Ryan was back in his role as ESPN analyst on Sunday, a few days after his arrest.
Ryan turned himself in to Nashville police on Wednesday on misdemeanor charges after he allegedly hit two pedestrians with his truck in a popular area downtown last week and then drove off after an argument, police said.
The former New York Jets and Buffalo Bills head coach was in ESPN’s studio for its three-hour “NFL Sunday Countdown” pregame show. Ryan didn’t address his arrest.
Ryan was driving a pickup truck when he allegedly ran over the feet of both individuals, who had the right of way crossing a main street in Nashville’s honky-tonk and music tourist district on Nov. 5, police said in a release Wednesday.
The pedestrians involved, who sustained minor injuries, waved Ryan down at another red light and said he stepped out to argue with them, according to police. They took a photo of the driver and the truck’s license plate, police said.
Ryan “immediately surrendered” himself to authorities after learning of the charges, his attorney, David Raybin, said Wednesday.
“From the outset, Coach Ryan has been fully cooperative with law enforcement and he intends to remain cooperative as the case moves forward,” Raybin said. “Because we just received the warrant today, we currently have limited information regarding the allegations.”
Ryan was charged with two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failure to give information or render aid and two counts of failure to obey a traffic control signal, according to court records. All are misdemeanors.
A judicial commissioner set Ryan’s bond at $6,000, but he qualified for pretrial release, according to the Davidson County Sheriff’s Office. That means he was released on non-financial conditions. He is scheduled to appear in court next month.
Ryan led the Jets to the AFC championship game in consecutive years after the 2009 and 2010 seasons.
While with the Jets, Ryan became one of the team’s — and the NFL’s — most popular figures, especially during his first few seasons as coach, because of his brash, colorful approach in news conferences that became must-watch TV.
He has not coached since being fired by the Bills with one game left in the 2016 season, though he has since expressed an interest in coaching and interviewed in 2025 for the Jets’ head coaching vacancy when Aaron Glenn was hired.
His father, the late Buddy Ryan, was an NFL coaching legend who famously coordinated the 1985 Chicago Bears defense that was one of the best in history. Seth Ryan, one of Rex Ryan’s two sons, is currently in his first season as the Jets’ passing game coordinator.
Ryan is best known now for his work at ESPN as one of the analysts on the network’s NFL pregame show.

title: Isaac, a cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse, has been reunited with his young owner
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday.
Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with the veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with 13-year-old Zariah Coleman.
It was a bit of good news amid the tragedy of Wednesday’s collapse, which killed 8 people, injured 18 others and forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, including one next door where Zariah lives.
Zariah and her mother told The New York Times on Sunday that workers found Isaac on Sunday in a cabinet under the kitchen sink of Zariah’s apartment after hearing a soft meow. Zariah and her family hadn’t been allowed in since the collapse, which tore off the side of her building and left a hole where her bedroom wall had been.
Waiting outside, Zariah hugged the cat’s cage as workers brought him out of her apartment building. Isaac had gone four days without food or water. After his rescue, he was taken to Flatbush Cats’ veterinary clinic for a checkup.
“I had it in my heart they would find Issac,” Zariah told the Times. “I knew they would.”
Zariah tearfully spoke about her missing cat at a news conference on Friday, telling reporters: “I just really hope they come and get our cat. He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani heralded Isaac and Zariah’s reunion in a social media post. He thanked Taylor’s office, the city’s Buildings Department and the nonprofit for the happy outcome.
“Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs,” Mamdani said. “We’re grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together.”

FBI warns of growing bank robbery trend where thieves install malware on ATMs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ST. FRANCIS, Wis. (WISN) - Two ATMs in Wisconsin were robbed of hundreds of thousands of dollars in a “jackpotting” scam that the FBI is calling a new way to rob a bank.
Video shows two men pulling up to an ATM at a Glendale bank in March. Instead of entering a pin number, one of them uses a key to get inside the machine. The screen goes black then appears to reboot before the men drive away.
About an hour later, video shows the men return to the ATM, and it looks like they hit the jackpot. They pull out stack after stack of money, fanning out the bills and boldly showing it off for a selfie.
Investigators are calling this method of “ATM jackpotting” a new way to rob a bank. Thieves hack into ATMs, tricking the machines into spitting out hundreds of thousands of dollars.
The thieves in the Glendale case got away with roughly $110,000. A week later, in another case in Greenfield, roughly $230,000 was stolen from a bank’s ATM. It’s unclear if the crimes were connected.
But the FBI says robbers like these are sophisticated criminals who install malware then hack ATMs to give out cash – and it’s a trend on the rise.
“Think of this as the new bank robbery, without the force of violence of a bank robbery,” said FBI Milwaukee Special Agent in Charge Alan Karr.
Karr says the thieves work for days surveilling the bank, its cameras and vulnerabilities before they strike.
Banks have reported more than 1,900 jackpotting incidents since 2020 across the United States. Last year alone, 700 incidents resulted in banks losing more than $20 million.
“We always encourage the banks to take common-sense approaches and measures, updating software to overcome vulnerabilities, increasing the physical protections of ATMs, cameras in the area,” Karr said.
Glendale police believe one of the suspects may be from Chicago as they work to identify those involved. Meanwhile, Greenfield police closed their case, saying they don’t have any leads.

title: Flu season is off to a very early start. Here’s where cases are surging right now
text:
NEW YORK (AP) - The U.S. flu season is off to a very early start, and it’s quickly intensifying.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday posted its latest update, reporting that seven states were reporting high flu activity last week, up from two states the week before.
The CDC also said that more than 3% of doctors’ office visits last week were for flu-like illness, signaling that flu season is really underway.
Louisiana is seeing the worst of it so far.
Flu season “is taking off and it’s taking off in a direction that’s only likely to increase in the next month or two,” said Dr. Fred Lopez, an infectious diseases specialist at the LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans.
“If you haven’t been vaccinated, you should get vaccinated now,” he added.
The early-season flu activity is higher than what’s usually seen at this point of the year, though it’s not clear that will mean this season will be worse than others, according to CDC’s update.
But not a good sign: The flu hospitalization rate in mid-October was the highest seen that early in an autumn in more than 15 years, noted Dr. Anna Durbin of Johns Hopkins University, during a recent media briefing.
The CDC estimates that at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations, and 2,100 deaths so far this season are tied to flu infections.
The surge began in the nation’s South and West, and the states seeing high flu activity so far include California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington, according to the CDC.
It’s not unusual for Louisiana to be among the first to see flu season surges each year. That is at least partly due to low vaccination rates, high poverty rates and challenges people face in accessing healthcare, Lopez said.
Doctors expect accelerated spread of flu and other respiratory viruses as people travel and gather later this month for Thanksgiving.
“As we prepare to gather with family and friends over the upcoming holidays, getting vaccinated is especially important,” said Dr. Nicole Iovine, a University of Florida-affiliated infectious disease specialist, in an emailed statement this week.
People should not get vaccinated if they are currently suffering significant symptoms, because the body’s immune system is otherwise occupied. But people should get a flu shot even if they already had an infection this fall, because the vaccine protects against three kinds of flu virus, and it’s not unusual for more than one strain to circulate each season, Lopez said.
Last winter’s flu season surged in late December and infections were especially intense in some parts of the country. At the time, New York City health officials called it the most intense season in 20 years.
The season faded in the following months, and was basically over by late March. But that spring the CDC estimated there had been at least 32 million illnesses, 380,000 hospitalizations and 24,000 deaths that season.
This fall, most of the illnesses so far are caused by a version of an A H1N1 flu bug with mutations that have the potential to more easily slip through the immune system’s defenses. However, data so far suggests the current vaccine “can recognize” the circulating virus and work against it, said Andrew Pekosz, a Johns Hopkins University immunology expert, during a recent media briefing.
Health officials won’t know for months exactly how effective this year’s vaccine is. But “right now there is no cause for concern,” he said.

title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft’s wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries.
The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 passenger aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said.
Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle.
On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft.
The NTSB said it was gathering information and may provide an update on Sunday.
The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said.
In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries.
UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened.
“We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.”
The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people.

text:
Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.
Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.
The company told The Associated Press that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business” and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations “that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” It did not address specific allegations.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement.
Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”
A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that “it doesn’t matter to me” whether Alice Huang is a spy. His concern is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions” or not.
“Jensen’s foibles are his foibles. Obviously, it’s a problem if in fact he was having relationships with subordinates,” Bessent said in an appearance on Fox News Channel’s “Sunday Futures.” “I want to keep coming back to: ‘What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?’”
Bessent said the Nvidia board of directors should look outside the company for a new CEO because “they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.”
Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.
Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company.
An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.
As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.
Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.
Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.
In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

title: 18-year-old high school student elected newest school board trustee
text:
(CNN) - An 18-year-old who is still in high school will be sworn in Thursday as the newest member of the Round Rock Independent School District Board of Trustees.
Ayaan Moledina, the district’s trustee-elect, has not yet received his high school diploma. Moledina said he turned 18 on Oct. 13.
A Round Rock native, Moledina will start as a freshman at the University of Texas in the fall while balancing his new role on the board.
Policy experience
Moledina said he has worked for congressmembers over the last 10 years. He also said he has worked on policy at the state Capitol to improve funding for schools and mental health.
“I found my passion for policymaking as my love language. As my ability to fix the problems that I see in the world,” Moledina said.
Election results
Moledina said he won 42% of the vote in a four-way race.
“People want fresh voices. People want something new, and my age doesn’t scare them because they know that I’m not coming out of nowhere,” he said.
Personal background
Moledina said his advocacy started with a diagnosis in the fifth grade.
Moledina is the child of Pakistani immigrants and is Muslim. He said he experienced racism and bullying growing up, which contributed to his major depressive disorder.
“The systems that I think were meant to support me were not doing so, not because of malicious intent by anybody, but because I think there was a huge lack of awareness,” he said.
Priorities as a trustee
Moledina said he hopes to work on suicide prevention and mental health awareness training for teachers in Round Rock, among other things, as a board member.
“One thing that I’ve heard over and over from parents is that we want less technology in the classroom, and iReady is part of that,” Moledina said. “And then I also want to make sure that we are funding special education, fine arts, talented and gifted, and our transportation services. We provide transportation for many of our homeless students.”
Moledina said he brings a student perspective to the board. He said that perspective is important because board decisions will affect students the most.
“My biggest hope is that fifth grade Ayaan, who was struggling so much, would be proud of what I’m doing today,” he said.

Norridgewock shooting range proposal continues to draw pushback
text:
NORRIDGEWOCK — Unbearable noise. Water contamination. Bald eagles scared away. Increased traffic.
Those were the chief concerns of neighbors of a proposed shooting range of up to 1,000 yards at 255 Skowhegan Road, who gathered at Mill Stream Elementary School on Thursday to urge the planning board to deny, or at least ask for information about, the site plan review application.
“Before you vote, I ask that you picture this long range was across from your home,” said Danielle Taylor, who lives on the other side of Skowhegan Road.
Most of the dozen residents who spoke at the hearing — many of whom have also submitted letters to the town — live next to the proposed range and are opposed to it. Two, who live elsewhere in town, spoke in favor of it.
“I hear gunfire all the time, every day — Saturday, Sunday, every day, all year round — I don’t care,” said Valerie Coulombe, of Winding Hill Road, adding she sees animals unaffected at another shooting range and the facility would be safer than shooting in gravel pits.
The planning board, which first began reviewing the project at its October meeting, did not discuss the project Thursday night after the public hearing. Town Manager Richard LaBelle said last week the board did not put it on the meeting’s agenda because developer Nicholas Carrier had yet to pay the application fee.
In September, Carrier objected to the town’s fee of $16,842.50, records show. In response, the select board revised the town’s fee schedule and came back with a new estimated fee of $2,139.75. The current fee has a $250 base, plus rates based on square footage of proposed pervious and impervious development.
Carrier also has not yet provided the board with all the information it requested at the last meeting, namely a stormwater management plan and a professional noise assessment.
Project consultant Stephen Gould, president of Sackett & Brake Survey in Skowhegan, said Thursday both of those were still in progress. He said he and Carrier were at the hearing simply to listen to feedback.
The planning board meets monthly, with its next regularly scheduled meeting Dec. 10.
Carrier, who owns NE Firearms, told the board previously the Skowhegan Road site would be an expansion of his business, currently run out of his home at 116 Goodwin Lane.
Plans submitted to the town call for a firearms store with a 25-yard test range in its rear. They also include 100-, 200-, 450- and 1,000-yard ranges to the south of the structure. The project is estimated to cost $190,000, records show.
There are no other ranges that long in the area, which could be a draw, Carrier said.
Deliberations over Carrier’s application come as voters narrowly rejected a proposed 180-day moratorium on certain noisy commercial developments, which would have paused the planning board’s review of the shooting range and a burnout pit off Ward Hill Road that has caused controversy.
The select board last week nevertheless discussed moving forward with exploring the idea of developing noise regulations to propose to voters. With only three of five members present at that meeting, Chair Matt Everett said he would bring up the issue again to the full board.
Some select board members and LaBelle have said there may have been confusion over the moratorium vote, and it is also possible some people may favornoise regulations but opposed putting them in place with two site plan applications already pending.
The planning board Thursday declined to take up the select board’s request to be involved in the process of developing the new rules.
Although the board heard many concerns Thursday, most focused on noise impacts from the potential constant use of high-powered firearms at the proposed range.
Carrier said in October that plans include natural sound buffers. And, he said, nearly all of his customers use suppressors on their firearms that soften the noise. He said he was also open to restrictions on his hours of operation and requiring suppressors on certain days.
Becky Sherburne, of Merry Farm Road, said she thinks the sound will travel up and down the Kennebec River. The noise would scare away local bald eagles neighbors enjoy seeing, she said.
“Why should something that’s only going to give a small population a good time disrupt our quiet lives?” Sherburne said. “I just see absolutely no way there’s going to be an economic impact great enough on Norridgewock to make up for us being held hostage.”
Others who spoke against the project were seeking more detailed information from Carrier.
“There’s just a lot of vagary here that will have no teeth if, two years from now, this is a problem,” said Chris Tibbetts, who lives across the Kennebec on the River Road.
Brad Farrin, who has lived on Skowhegan Road with his family his whole life, urged the planning board to request a safety analysis, engineered berm plans, a noise study, a lead management plan, a stormwater and erosion control plan, a wildlife habitat review and a review of state environmental protection permitting regulations.
Farrin, a Republican finishing a term in the state Senate, said in his written comments that if the board approves the plans, it should require regular reporting, monitoring and inspections and define a process to respond to complaints.
Farrin said he also contacted the Maine State Police to see if officials were interested in using the range for training, as Carrier told the planning board previously.
Sgt. Paul Casey of the firearms training unit confirmed the agency had been in touch with Carrier, Farrin said, but told Farrin the agency does not take a position on specific projects. State police spokesperson Maj. Aaron Turcotte said Friday via text message he was busy and unable to respond to say whether that was accurate.
“If this range begins successful operations, we may look into its use, but again, we may not,” Casey said, according to Farrin. “I guess what I’m trying to say is that I would not want the state police, as an organization, to hold weight on you or your residents’ opinions or concerns.”
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Jake Freudberg can be reached at jfreudberg@centralmaine.com.

title: Trump's handpicked party chair faces a rebellion as midterm losses challenge president's grip on GOP
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump’s handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it’s already getting ugly.
Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump’s former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don’t fall in line.
The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump’s dominance, even after the party’s worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the heavy losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies.
But inside the RNC, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party’s national political operation, a small yet growing group is backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge.
The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky’s KC Crosbie, the RNC’s second-in-command, who launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters’ allies.
Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his “Make America Great Again” agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power.
“We have an obligation to serve the Republican Party the most effective way we can. And if all we do is say yes to what the White House wants, I’m not sure that’s doing what’s best for the Republican Party,” said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie’s candidacy. “Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time.”
He said that requires a change in leadership.
“There’s so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn’t pull his weight in this election, that the RNC was far less effective than it should have been,” he said.
In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as “a serious setback” and called for the RNC to provide “an honest account” of what went wrong.
“We should preserve what we built and be equally willing to confront where we fell short,” she wrote.
Crosbie declined to be interviewed. The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC’s winter meeting in Arizona.
Inside the rebellion against Gruters
It’s unclear how many RNC members will back Crosbie, although the number so far is believed to be small. Some would-be supporters privately acknowledge that they’re worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump’s new White House chief of staff. Others believe in the committee’s tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs.
Gruters also has vocal backers.
Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised the chairman’s leadership and his efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this election cycle.
She described Gruters as “highly responsive” during the campaign and praised his “record-setting fundraising.”
“From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job,” she said, adding that Trump’s endorsement is “something that the committee should take very seriously.”
Nevada Republican Party Chairman Michael McDonald called Crosbie a “dear friend,” but said Trump is “the leader of our party” and “you always have to fall in line with the leader.”
“I don’t have a bad word to say about KC at all. It’s just that the president wants to go with Joe Gruters,” he said. “The president made his choice.”
The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in conservative strongholds such as Texas, South Carolina and Mississippi.
Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be “catastrophic” and “insulting” to the party’s base “to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don’t need to do anything different, that we don’t need new players and a new plan.”
Lyman described Crosbie as “by far the best candidate currently running to lead the RNC forward to victory in 2028.”
Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — for a total of 20 — at the committee’s January meeting. That number is the minimum required for a successful nomination.
She insisted that she wouldn’t be scared off by backlash from Trump or the White House, which has been actively lobbying RNC members.
“We should not be influenced by any one person or other. It’s our organization,” Cienki said. “We have to hold an election, not a selection.”
Trump is furious with Crosbie
Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie’s Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up.
During a White House meeting Nov. 6, Trump threatened to punish the RNC if members crossed him and said he would refuse to help the organization, including appearing at fundraisers or allowing his name and image to be used in mail and digital solicitations. That’s according to a senior White House official with direct knowledge of the meeting who was not authorized to publicly discuss the private gathering and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Such a threat would be catastrophic to the party because Trump remains its most effective money raiser.
An Axios story that first reported the threats was distributed via text message to all 168 RNC members.
The same senior White House official said staff convinced Trump that he should not go after Crosbie personally that day. Instead, he released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a “MAGA Warrior” and giving him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
The leadership fight comes as Trump has shown no interest in relinquishing power
The Constitution bars Trump from seeking a third term, but he is expected to play a central role in picking the party’s next presidential nominee. Trump’s team contends that he remains the most popular Republican in the country, and House Republicans this week elected a slate of new leaders closely aligned with him.
The White House referred questions about the leadership fight to Trump’s Truth Social post.
The party’s future is at stake
The RNC will oversee the party’s presidential primary process, including setting the nominating calendar, the debate schedule, the national convention and the rules governing the selection of the White House candidate.
People close to Gruters, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations, said Crosbie’s campaign was “100% a challenge” to the president’s power and described the RNC as “the president’s political operation.”
Allies argued that a leadership change now would put the RNC at a severe disadvantage heading into the next presidential cycle because a new team would need time to get up to speed and they warned that friction between the president and the committee’s leadership would curtail their ability to organize and raise money.
They also rejected Crosbie’s call for a postelection review, which they said would do little more than rehash the past and put all their grievances on paper. Similar demands for a retrospective were a headache for Ken Martin, the embattled leader of the Democratic National Committee, after Trump won in 2024.
But they said Gruters has taken the criticism seriously and has been soliciting feedback to make adjustments heading into 2028.
Gruters spent much of this week holding private phone conversations with committee members. Those who participated in the calls said Gruters listened to their grievances but said little about what he would do differently.
Spending faces scrutiny
The opposition to Trump’s choice to lead the RNC has little to do with Trump’s leadership or policy decisions, according to nearly a half-dozen Crosbie supporters.
Instead, they focused on the RNC’s spending decisions under Gruters. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still lost the House and Senate.
“There’s clearly a groundswell of support for a forensic audit,” said Brock, the RNC member from Tennessee.
In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns.
Gruters defended a $22,500 expenditure for hospitality space at the Presidents Cup, a golf event, saying it was offered to major donors and “resulted in $2.5 million in renewed contributions to the RNC.”
He also addressed concerns about “a brief contract” between the RNC and Caroline Wiles, a longtime Republican consultant who is the daughter of Susie Wiles, Trump’s former chief of staff. Gruters said she was hired by his predecessor at the committee, Michael Whatley.
“While I have no reason to doubt Caroline Wiles’s value to the RNC or Chairman Whatley’s reasons for bringing her on, this was a brief six-month engagement that ended when I was elected Chairman,” he wrote.
Gruters also defended the RNC’s decision to pay for “hair and make-up services” for senior White House officials, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
“This was a request made of us so that the expense did not fall to taxpayers,” Gruters wrote. He said the beneficiaries “generously gave so much of their limited time and energies to help the RNC this cycle” and “did not ask for much of us in return, so we felt this was a request we could accommodate.”
Gruters promised to provide members “honest and direct answers to concerns raised” as conversations continue.
“I pledge to listen and learn from you about what happened in the field,” he wrote, “so together we can move forward stronger than ever.”

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline trave l this weekend, using the incident to push Congress on money to fully upgrade America’s air traffic control system.
The Republican president has been conspicuously quiet on the ground stop since it began Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.
Trump said in a new post on his social media platform that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in “drips and drabs.” The Republican-controlled Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Federal Aviation Administration as part of the party’s sweeping tax cut package last year, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly characterized that funding as an down payment on a broader overhaul of the aging system.
“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trump wrote on social media Sunday. “It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old – RIDICULOUS!”
In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing Joe Biden’s administration of making an “old and broken system worse than when they began.”
Biden signed a massive infrastructure bill into law in the first year of his presidency, which set aside $25 billion for the FAA to improve airports and its traffic control towers, to redevelop airport terminals, to “upgrade the foundation” of the air traffic control system, according to the FAA.
Duffy was the administration’s public face on the ground stop across the Sunday news shows, pressing Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air traffic control infrastructure.
In a post on the social media platform X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. had secured two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting “deep diagnostics” on the equipment. He has said the problem began when L3Harris was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload.
As for the traveling public, he told CBS’ “Face the Nation” that “we have some delays in the airspace right now,” but looking to the end of the day and into Monday, “we should be running at full capacity.”

Van Hollen, a two-term incumbent who previously represented the state in the House and in the legislature, launched his bid Thursday, casting himself as a new face that reflects the public’s desire for change after the midterm campaign delivered Democrats control of the Senate and the House.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people,” he said in a statement.
The election is set for early December and will be held behind closed doors, with voting done through secret ballot. Schumer, a five-term incumbent, has been the longtime leader of the caucus and serves as minority leader. He was majority leader from 2021 to 2025, during Democrat Joe Biden’s presidency, and has projected confidence he has the votes to prevail.
Van Hollen has gotten support from a few high-profile members of the Democratic caucus. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, has backed him, saying he leads with courage and experience, as has Michigan’s incoming senator, Abdul El-Sayed. Schumer had backed El-Sayed’s primary challenger, Haley Stevens, who at the end of the general election campaign backed Republican Mike Rogers.
An attorney and legislator, Van Hollen was born in Karachi, Pakistan, amid his parents’ diplomatic service there, and he captured attention early in Trump’s second term when he pushed back against the administration’s immigration agenda.
He traveled some 2,000 miles (3,200 kilometers) to El Salvador to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was wrongly deported and who federal courts said should be returned. Van Hollen did not secure the release of the Salvadoran citizen who was living in Maryland. But meeting with him, in defiance of Trump, Van Hollen helped establish hope and momentum for Abrego Garcia’s family and captured national press attention.
With Maryland home to numerous federal agencies and workers, Van Hollen has been a vocal opponent of Trump’s cuts, including those at NASA, the National Institutes of Health and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, among others.

text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The painting was buried behind coats and boxes in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades.
Few if anyone knew about the hidden treasure until the woman in her 90s who lived there nonchalantly told her niece one day, “oh by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
The painting — an early example from a time when O’Keeffe became enamored with the American Southwest — depicts a classic New Mexico landscape with rolling hills in earth tones.
Christie’s estimates its value at $3 to $5 million. It is set to go up for auction on Tuesday.
The auction house says the painting from 1930 was likely the first in a series of three. The second is in New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. The other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family.
Up until now, the whereabouts of the first one had largely been a mystery.
O’Keeffe painting comes from a key period
The painting of Lobo Peak near Taos, New Mexico, is “particularly important because of its early date and its representation of the inception point of O’Keeffe’s time in the American Southwest,” said Tylee Abbott, director of American Art at Christie’s.
In 1963, a New York art gallery sold the painting for $3,800 to a woman who gave it to her daughter.
“Before that it was only known through photography that had been taken in 1931,” Abbott said.
O’Keeffe, who died in 1986 at age 98, is often called the “Mother of American modernism.” She was a pioneer with her own style of abstract art, most known for paintings of flowers and Southwestern landscapes.
She lived in Abiquiu, New Mexico, where she built a home and studio on land with breathtaking desert vistas that inspired the work of the 20th century painter. Many Native American communities trace their ancestry to the area in northern New Mexico.
Family believes painting was a graduation gift
The daughter of the woman who purchased the painting in 1963 kept it at her apartment in New York’s East Village, the auction house said. The family has asked the auction house not to release their identities.
But they did share with Christie’s some details, including how the artwork was found.
The woman who owned the painting lived into her late 90s before dying recently. Never married, she was extremely private and incredibly smart, the family said. At one point in her life, she worked with the U.S. Foreign Service, spending time in Europe.
She collected antiques and abstract art but nothing close to the stature of the O’Keeffe.
The family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother after earning a master’s degree in the 1960s. For many years, she displayed it until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely.
Painting has O’Keeffe’s signature mark
She boxed it back into the original packing crate and put it in the back of a closet, said her niece, who spent the last few years caring for her and spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to honor the family’s request for privacy.
Around 2022, the woman first mentioned to her niece that the painting was in the front closet. It stayed there until this year when they were cleaning out the apartment and getting her affairs in order.
Once unboxed, it was obvious the painting was authentic.
It has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work — including her signature marking on the back, a star with her initials “OK” scrawled in the middle.
___
Seewer reported from Ohio.

KYLE, Texas (KEYE) — Kyle police announced a second officer died following Sunday’s crash in Comal County.

The driver, Officer Austin Brennan, was taken to the hospital and died from his injuries Thursday.
What the Texas Department of Public Safety said
The Texas Department of Public Safety said a white Ford F-250 was heading north on FM 1102 when it left the road.
The driver overcorrected, and the truck slid sideways before rolling over. Three other passengers were injured.
Remembering Brennan
Brennan’s former next-door neighbor, Carlos Samudio, said Brennan was someone who was always willing to lend a hand, on or off duty.

Samudio said he wondered if Brennan was involved when he heard about the crash.
“I was like, oh my gosh, I wonder if that was Austin because I heard the vehicle was a Ford 250, which he had,” Samudio said.
Samudio remembers Brennan’s love for the outdoors, his motorcycle and his dog, Chief.
“If you knew him, you would totally just be enamored with his aura. Like he just would bring people in,” Samudio said.
Service with the department
Kyle police said Guzman served in the department for 10 years and received numerous awards, including multiple life-saving and meritorious conduct awards.

Samudio extended his condolences to Kyle police and the community.

title: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
text:
Maybe the trouble started with the AI billionaire and the Silicon Valley chaos that followed talk of his infidelity, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Or maybe it was the Microsoft outage that, depending on how you looked at it, either cast millions of frustrated workers adrift or spared them from a daily, unrelenting electronic avalanche.
But by Friday afternoon, when U.S. authorities suddenly ordered every plane across the country to land immediately, it felt to many that something was up. Something was broken.
Just ask Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, trying to fly out of Newark Liberty International Airport when his canceled flight led to a few beers with his brother in an airport bar and eventually a night in a hotel. Saturday morning, he was back at the airport to try again.
“There’s a lot of weird stuff going on,” Amasio said. “It makes one think.”
His first thought was dark: “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore. They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”
Throw in a few more examples just from Friday – a cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans when a tanker slammed into it, suspicious drones over a U.S. air base in Britain, a bomb found near an ethanol plant in Ohio — and perhaps things seem even weirder, opening the door for a writer who has been picking at America’s fears for generations to offer his own explanation.
“The aliens have landed,” Stephen King wrote in a Friday afternoon tweet. “That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”
The official explanations for the thousands of downed jetliners and hours of email and other computer troubles were far more prosaic.
A technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system had overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours, administration officials said.
By Saturday morning, air travel was already smoother and Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said airline schedules should be back to normal by late Sunday.
Microsoft, for its part, said Saturday that its services had been fully restored, saying the problem “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.
The outage is believed to have affected many millions of people around the world.
‘Is this a cyberattack?’
Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was in line to pick up a hastily booked rental car at Chicago’s O’Hare airport on Friday afternoon so she and colleagues could get home from a work training.
Gustafson said the week’s mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.
“It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.”
Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity had been behind the troubles.
Tori Perkins, 34, was hoping for a Saturday flight at Terminal 2 at San Diego International Airport, where 11 of the 62 flights already were listed as canceled that morning and the same number were delayed. Crowds were normal.
“It’s one of those things where I don’t necessarily believe what the government says,” said Perkins, who seemed to take the setback in stride. “I don’t know what’s true because there are so many people saying different things.”
Perkins, who lives in Hawaii, was in San Diego on a layover on her way to see family in Florida. She spent Friday night at the airport.
She was not surprised that Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy had made a plea Friday for tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the country’s notoriously outdated air traffic system.
“It sounds like more of the same,” she said.
The FAA has already replaced thousands of copper wire connections with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. The White House has been pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Bright spots ease concerns
Sometimes chaos brings out the best in people.
Corbyn Wascher was stuck on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours while heading back to Moline, Illinois, from Miami, where he had been at an education conference.
He said everyone was cordial on the plane, talking to one another and stretching their legs. He was impressed with the American Airlines staff, who handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, though they were clearly under stress.
“The stewardesses were amazing,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher.
Back at the Newark airport, Caroline Ruiz had caught a few hours of sleep by a heating vent. She wasn’t sure what time it was as she waited for someone to bring her a meal she was promised after the cancellation of the first leg of her 24-hour trip to Australia. She hoped to get started later Saturday.
It was two days in a row, she noted, where she had been betrayed by technology.
Though maybe one of those days didn’t count as a betrayal.
“I kind of got a free day yesterday” because the Microsoft systems were down.
___
Associated Press journalists Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Ali Swenson in Chicago, Jessica Hill in Las Vegas and Aron Ranen in Newark contributed to this report.

title: Apple, pecan and pumpkin dessert recipes for your Thanksgiving

This story was originally published in November 2020.
When it comes to Thanksgiving desserts, there are a number of classics that always seem to find a way to the table. More often than not, it’s pies — apple, pecan or pumpkin are perhaps the most prevalent — that are duking it out for that center spot.
Here are desserts that use either apples, pecans or pumpkins (or perhaps a combination of them) that will make your Thanksgiving extra sweet this year, no matter how you’re celebrating.
Apple custard pie
An apple custard pie is a decadent alternative to a classic apple pie. The creamy custard filling may make this recipe seem gourmet, but is simple to prepare even for novice home chefs. Here’s how to make apple custard pie.
Pumpkin pecan pie
The combination of pumpkin and pecan is a spin on the classic pies that grace the Thanksgiving table. With a hint of maple, you can’t get much better for a Maine Thanksgiving. Here is a recipe for pumpkin pecan pie.
Apple squares
With light fluffy pastry, sweet apples and a creamy custard in the center, each of these apple squares is like an autumnal slice of heaven. Preparing this recipe for apple squares will make a delicious addition to any Thanksgiving table.
Flourless apple dessert
Based on a reader recipe from a mid-twentieth century tea house, this flourless apple dessert is not only a good way to avoid gluten, but also provides a lighter, no-less-delicious dessert for those of us willing to admit that we’re unlikely to enjoy anything too rich after a hearty Thanksgiving meal. You can eat it warm with ice cream, and also enjoy it the next day for breakfast. Check out this tasty recipe for flourless apple dessert.
Pumpkin bars
These tasty pumpkin bars with a sweet cream cheese frosting are easy to whip up from a can of pumpkin puree. You can even spice it up with a little extra cinnamon or ginger, or swap out a simple vanilla frosting or even a sprinkle of confectioners’ sugar to mix it up. Here is a recipe for iced pumpkin bars that would make for a delicious dessert on Thanksgiving.
Apple cake
Apple cake is yet another versatile dessert that will be delicious the night of Thanksgiving, but equally enjoyable in the days to come with a cup of coffee for breakfast or as a snack after lunch — that is, if you don’t finish it all on Thanksgiving night. Check out this recipe for apple cake to see for yourself.
Pumpkin chocolate chip cookies
Cookies might be a better fit for a small Thanksgiving. These pumpkin chocolate chip cookies are a delicious way to bring a little chocolatey goodness into the classic Turkey Day palette. Here is the recipe for pumpkin chocolate chip cookies.
Pecan cookies
Pecans give these cookies a delicious texture and flavor. If you master them, they will be great for Christmas, too. Here is the recipe for shortbread pecan cookies.
