text:
The Fall Five and Five: County Athletes Earn Postseason Honors
Before I start counting down the five stories that defined the fall sports season, there is one more piece of the season that deserves some attention.
Actually, quite a bit of it.
Over the last couple of weeks, postseason honors have started rolling in for athletes from across Aroostook County. Soccer players have been recognized for everything from performance and sportsmanship to regional all-star selections. Cross country runners have landed on all-conference teams after championship seasons of their own.
So before the Five and Five countdown begins Monday, this is my honorable mention.
Not one game. Not one athlete.
This one belongs to all of the County athletes who earned recognition for the seasons they put together.
Butch Shaw Awards Recognize More Than the Scoreboard
We'll start with an honor that has meant something in Aroostook County soccer for 40 years.
Ten County soccer players received the 2026 Butch Shaw Awards, presented by the Northern Maine Board of Approved Soccer Officials to players who exemplify sportsmanship and respect along with their play on the field.
The girls recipients were Lilly Burtt of Central Aroostook, Madisyn Cyr and Emma Soucy of Wisdom, Reece Doucette of Fort Kent and Ava Ezell of Houlton.
On the boys side, Dominic Cyr of Fort Kent, Bodey McPherson of Presque Isle, Drew Lamoreau of Easton, Levi Cole of Fort Fairfield and Cooper Willard of Houlton received the honor.
The award has always been about something bigger than statistics.
It was established in memory of Clyde "Butch" Shaw, and the qualities attached to his name still matter four decades later: competing hard, respecting the game and representing your school the right way.
County Runners Fill the PVC Cross Country Teams
Cross country produced some of the best County performances of the entire fall, so it probably shouldn't be surprising to see local runners all over the PVC postseason teams.
On the Large School girls First Team, Emma Graves and Jenna Strid of Caribou joined Lillian Johnson and Aleah Rideout of Presque Isle.
The Second Team included Isabella Albert of Caribou and Marie Johnston and Taylor York of Presque Isle, while Abra Connell of Presque Isle earned honorable mention.
Graves was also named the PVC Large School Girls Runner of the Year, while Caribou's Thomas Beckham earned Coach of the Year honors.
The Large School boys selections included Paxton Darrell of Presque Isle and Peyton Gorneault and Tewolde Stewart of Caribou on the First Team.
Jeremy Charette and Geonni Guevara of Presque Isle made the Second Team, with Isaac Brissette and Xander Jamieson of Caribou and Henry Clayton and Connor Miele of Presque Isle earning honorable mention.
State champion Pierce Gorneault of Caribou was named Large School Boys Runner of the Year, Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero earned Coach of the Year, and Houlton/GHCA's Nathan Brady received the Boys PVC Inspirational Award.
The Small School teams had plenty of Houlton/GHCA representation as well.
Brayden Drake, Wyatt Quint, Logan Witmer and Malachi Witmer all landed on the boys First Team. Brady was named to the Second Team and Stephen Cormier earned honorable mention.
Malachi Witmer was named PVC Small School Boys Runner of the Year, with Houlton/GHCA's Chris Rines earning Coach of the Year.
On the girls side, Charlotte Estabrook of Houlton/GHCA received Small School honorable mention.
That's a lot of County names, and it follows a season that included conference titles, regional championships, a state championship and a state runner-up finish.
Presque Isle and Caribou Lead the County's Class B Soccer Honors
The Class B PVC soccer teams brought another long list of County selections.
For the boys, Caribou's Declan Miller joined Jackson Greaves, Trenton Mastro and Bodey McPherson of Presque Isle on the First Team.
The Second Team included Louie Hebert and Carter St. Peter of Caribou, along with Pruet Dionne of Presque Isle.
On the girls side, Peyton Boinske and Hailey Plant of Presque Isle were First Team selections.
Quinn Corrigan and Lilly Bell of Caribou and Emily Collins of Presque Isle earned Second Team honors.
It was another reminder of how much County talent was competing in Class B this fall, including a Presque Isle girls team that reached the Northern Maine championship game.
More County Honors in Class C and Eight-Player Soccer
Fort Kent and Houlton also had plenty of names on the PVC's Class C, Class D and Eight-Player postseason lists.
For the Class C boys, Dominic Cyr, Finley Marquis and Kyle Paradis of Fort Kent earned First Team recognition, with Caleb Saucier receiving honorable mention.

Reagan Wright of Houlton and Laney Caron and Avery Werntgen of Fort Kent landed on the Second Team.

In Eight-Player boys soccer, Cooper Willard of Houlton earned First Team honors and Carter Smith was named to the Third Team. Houlton's Michael Zykowski was selected as Coach of the Year.
The Spirit of the Game selections also included County athletes, with Dominic Cyr and Kiley Marquis of Fort Kent and Cameron Smith and Allie Worthley of Houlton among those recognized.
Forty-Seven County Players Earn Regional All-Star Recognition
Then came another major round of soccer honors.
The Maine Soccer Coaches Association released its 2026 Regional All-Star teams, and 47 Aroostook County players were selected across the boys and girls divisions.
On the girls side, the Northern Class B team included Peyton Boinske and Hailey Plant of Presque Isle.
Class C included Laney Caron, Reese Doucette and Avery Werntgen of Fort Kent, along with Ava Ezell and Morgan Quirk of Houlton/GHCA.
The Class D selections included Addison Labelle and Sadie Trams of Ashland; Lilly Burtt and Charlie Pierce of Central Aroostook; Adrianna Bridges of Fort Fairfield; Norah Carter and Ivy Schmeling of Madawaska; and Emily Lapierre of Van Buren.

The Eight-Player boys team included Carter Smith and Cooper Willard of Houlton/GHCA, Conor Schmidt of Katahdin, and James Desjardins, Cayden Hartsgrove and Preston Lavoie of Wisdom.
For the seniors on those regional teams, there's one more opportunity to put on the uniform. They're invited to participate in the Senior Game Sunday, November 15, at Thomas College.
Before We Count Down the Five
There are plenty of championship moments coming over the next five days.
But I didn't want to start the countdown without recognizing just how many County athletes put together seasons worthy of recognition outside their own schools and communities.
Some won championships.
Some put up huge numbers.
Some were asked to anchor a defense, control the midfield, make the save or get their team through five kilometers as quickly as they possibly could.
Others were recognized because of how they carried themselves while doing it.
They all became part of what made the fall of 2026 such a memorable season to cover.
So this is where the season-ending Five and Five begins.
Honorable Mention: The athletes who represented Aroostook County on postseason honor rolls across Maine.
Starting Monday, we'll begin counting down the five stories that defined the fall.
Five days.
Five stories.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange.
The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor.
The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.
Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.
Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.
U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.

title: New bodycam video shows moments after college student’s 8-story fall from apartment window
text:
ATHENS, Ga. (ANF/Gray News) - Newly released video offers a closer look at the chaotic aftermath and miraculous survival of a Georgia college student who fell eight stories from her apartment window.
Kristin Sargent, a 21-year-old senior at the University of Georgia, was dancing on furniture Sept. 26 when she lost her balance and fell from her eighth-floor apartment window. The fall was about 65 to 70 feet, according to newly obtained video and 911 audio.
“My friend just fell out of the window on the eighth floor,” a caller told a 911 dispatcher immediately following the incident. “We were dancing, and she just fell out the window.”
The fall happened during Georgia-Oklahoma weekend, when several friends were staying at Sargent’s five-person apartment at the Rambler Athens building, an off-campus complex.
Apartment security camera video captured Sargent falling, with the window screen following her. The 21-year-old survived the fall but suffered a number of injuries.
“We were dancing, and we were singing ‘The Climb’ by Miley Cyrus,” said a roommate in body camera footage released by Athens-Clarke County Police. “We had our glass up, but the screen was down. She was dancing and fell backward.”
First responders arrived on the scene to find Sargent conscious and able to speak, despite the height of the fall. A police officer said she had an open femur fracture and blood coming from a wound in her chest.
“I thought I was coming down here to see her dead. Have you seen anything like this before? I think it was a miracle the fact that she wasn’t dead,” said one of Sargent’s friends in the bodycam footage.
Police noted that patio furniture located near the apartment complex’s swimming pool likely broke Sargent’s fall and saved her life. Investigators documented blood and a broken armrest on the cushioned metal bench.
“We all were like, ‘If anyone was going to come back from this, it’s Kristin,’” a roommate said in the bodycam footage.
Another of Sargent’s roommates told police that the 21-year-old had been at a bar during the Georgia-Oklahoma game. A hospital administrator later described her as “drunk.” A police officer said her condition might have contributed to her body not bracing as she fell.
Sargent faces an extended recovery, but family and friends say her survival is nothing short of remarkable.

title: 32 Americans named as Rhodes scholars have variety of interests, from space junk to art history
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A college senior who wants to clean up debris pollution in Earth’s orbit and a student who has researched AI use in healthcare are among the 32 Americans named as 2027 Rhodes scholars.
The winners, who were announced on Saturday, have a variety of interests, from bioelectronics to water scarcity to art history. They were chosen from 238 finalists who emerged from more than 1,000 candidates who received formal endorsements from their colleges and universities for the honor.
The students will attend the University of Oxford in England as part of the Rhodes scholar program, which awards more than 100 scholarships worldwide each year for students to pursue two to three years of graduate studies.
Two students are the first-ever Rhodes scholars from their schools — Prairie View A&M University in Texas and The Citadel — The Military College of South Carolina. Harvard University led the way with four 2027 Rhodes scholars, followed by Yale and Princeton with three each.
The winners include:
Evan Garrison, of Webb City, Missouri, a senior at Mississippi State University majoring in aerospace engineering and mathematics. His research includes designing ways to detect objects in space, with an interest in cleaning up orbital debris known as “space junk.” He plans to study mathematical modeling, scientific computing and global governance and diplomacy at Oxford.
Asuka Koda, of New York City, a senior at Yale University majoring in mathematics and philosophy. She has researched AI adoption in healthcare and has been a health and science writer for CNN. She plans to study social science of the internet and international health and tropical medicine at Oxford.
Michael Bueker, from Wellesley, Massachusetts, a senior at Dartmouth College majoring in biomedical engineering. His research has focused on biodegradable, implantable neural stimulators and other ultrathin bioelectronic devices. He also grows giant pumpkins. At Oxford, he intends to study engineering science.
Elizabeth Koenck, of Aurora, Colorado, a senior at Georgetown University majoring in foreign service. Her research has examined water scarcity problems across the Middle East, North Africa and the Colorado River Basin. She plans to pursue degrees in migration studies and water science, policy and management at Oxford.
Sabrina Soriano, of Azusa, California, a senior at Yale University majoring in art history. Her research includes 19th-century French painting, with a focus on the relationship between art, religion and cultural identity. She plans to study history of art and visual culture and visual, material and museum anthropology at Oxford.
Named after British imperialist and benefactor Cecil John Rhodes, the scholarships were established at Oxford in 1903. The program has more than 8,000 alumni, many of whom have pursued careers in government, education, the arts and social justice.

Trump breaks silence on nationwide ground stop and demands more money from Congress
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is pressing for $50 billion to address an aging air traffic control system after problems with routers apparently led to a rare nationwide grounding of all planes, but Democrats are demanding answers about how the administration has spent billions it’s already been given and why its funding request has soared.
The growing rift over how to address the Federal Aviation Administration’s vulnerabilities comes as passengers across the country are struggling to get to where they need to go after thousands of flights were grounded Friday, and investigators are still trying to figure out what went wrong.
President Donald Trump, who hadn’t spoken publicly or commented on the flight grounding, finally weighed in Sunday with comments on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and calling for more money to pay for improvements to the system.
The finger-pointing and blame-shifting between the Republican administration and Democrats in Congress underscored the political division that could only grow wider when Democrats take control in January and scrutiny of the Trump administration accelerates, even on a matter that impacts all travelers.
During appearances on Sunday morning talk shows, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy detailed what is known — and still unclear — about the problems that led up to his decision Friday to ground the planes, as he also pushed Congress for billions more to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades.
Duffy details what happened
In a post on X, Duffy said the problem began when a federal contractor was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, causing the system to overload.
After the wire was replaced at the site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, cascading into the ground stop.
The FAA said in a statement that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said. The contractor blocked the two locations in Arkansas and Texas, and the agency said that stabilized the network.
Duffy said billions are needed to build a “brand new architecture” for the network and said companies — including AT&T, Verizon and Lumen — are ready to deploy it “tomorrow” if the money is there.
Aging air traffic control system has been a problem for years
The need to upgrade the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years.
Under President Joe Biden, Congress approved a massive infrastructure bill that included $25 billion over five years for airport and air traffic control infrastructure improvements. Much of that money went to airports for such things as new runways and taxiways, and new and refurbished terminals.
Under Trump, a Republican-led Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize the FAA’s air traffic system.
The administration said the money would provide critical updates to outdated radar systems and traffic control centers, some dating back to the 1960s. Republicans used the same bill to allocate $170 billion for Trump’s immigration crackdown, for more border security and immigration enforcement.
In a hearing on Sept. 15, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said with the money Congress provided, “we are executing on the most ambitious modernization and delivering it in record time.”
The FAA upgrade has two phases. The first, funded by the $12.5 billion, is supposed to be completed by December 2028. A second phase involves developing new systems to track aircraft and optimize traffic. Bedford told lawmakers in September that the second phase will cost at least an additional $10 billion.
Separately, Sen. Eric Schmitt, a Missouri Republican, in September introduced a bill that builds on the $12.5 billion Congress approved last year and calls for about $30 billion more in new investments in the nation’s air transportation system. Duffy has also pushed for that funding.
Schmitt’s bill would include the $10 billion Bedford said is needed for the second phase. On top of that it includes money to modernize up to three medium hub airports and to make various airport improvements around the country, from new air traffic control towers to new terminals.
Then on Friday Duffy said he wants $50 billion, but he hasn’t detailed what it’s for. He said Saturday that he’ll be sending a detailed request to legislators on Monday.
Democrats question rising costs and why money hasn’t been spent
Congressional Democrats say they also want to upgrade the country’s aging air traffic control system. But they are questioning the price tag.
Democrats on the House Transportation Committee said most of the money appropriated last year remains unspent.
“Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” Rep. Rick Larsen, the ranking Democrat on the committee, and Rep. André Carson, the top Democrat on a subcommittee with jurisdiction over aviation issues, said in a statement.
Democrats on the House Appropriations Committee are asking the same question. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the panel, said Congress has shown it’s willing to invest in modernizing the FAA.
“But we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner. Right now, it is clear that we lack such a partner,” DeLauro said.
Duffy said Sunday the money appropriated last year by Congress will be spent by the end of 2028. He also said his agency was restricted by Congress in how it could be spent and that didn’t include spending on the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure.
Trump conspicuously quiet for 2 days
Trump had not commented publicly or on social media after the ground stop was ordered Friday afternoon, although he was active on social media about unrelated matters.
Sunday morning, he weighed in with a post on Truth Social, saying his administration has begun upgrading the air traffic control system but it should not be done in “drips and drabs.”
“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trump wrote. “It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!”
Duffy said Trump has been “fully engaged” on the ground stop.
Travel should return to normal by Monday
As for the traveling public, Duffy said that “as we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity.”
Duffy said the administration feels “pretty good” that the breakdown did not result from a hacking event. He said various intelligence agencies have said they were not finding the “chatter or the footprints that we would normally see if this was a cyberattack.”
Duffy appeared on CBS’ “Face the Nation,” CNN’s “State of the Union,” “Fox News Sunday,” NBC’s “Meet the Press” and ABC’s “This Week.”

Democrats are weighing impeachment of RFK Jr. while courting his supporters
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — When Democrats take over Congress in January, one of their many oversight targets will be Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose overhaul of longstanding vaccine guidance and cuts to medical research over the past two years have drawn fiery criticism. Some high-ranking lawmakers have suggested impeaching him.
But those efforts could conflict with another growing priority for many lawmakers on the left: nurturing areas of common ground with Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again followers with the aim of securing their political support.
It could prove a difficult balance, since many MAHA activists whom Democrats are courting as part of their new coalition still view Kennedy as their closest ally.
“It’s an unenviable position for Democrats to be in,” said Matt Motta, a professor at Boston University School of Public Health. In addition to treading carefully not to upset MAHA voters, Motta said, the lawmakers will also have to answer to a left-leaning base that wants more accountability from Kennedy on vaccines as measles outbreaks surge around the country.
Some members of the MAHA movement said they’re eager to work with Democrats to pass legislation on shared interests, like regulating pesticides and making school lunches healthier. But extensive investigations into Kennedy, or hostility toward him, could complicate those collaborations.
“I’m not saying that the Democratic leadership can’t continue to have an irrational war on Secretary Kennedy until they collapse,” said Mark Gorton, president of the Kennedy-aligned MAHA Institute. “But when they do that, they alienate all the MAHA voters out there, the people who really care about fighting corporate capture.”
Democrats are ready to hold Kennedy’s feet to the fire
Kennedy, a lifelong Democrat before running for president as an independent in 2024 and then throwing his support behind President Donald Trump’s campaign, has repeatedly clashed with his former party since joining the Trump administration.
Democrats have assailed his Health and Human Services Department for sweeping staffing cuts unleashed as part of Trump’s government efficiency push and for the decision to eliminate areas of scientific study that the administration deemed too focused on diversity, equity and inclusion.
They’ve also grilled him in congressional hearings over his efforts to change government vaccine policies while sidestepping long-held protocols for that reform.
Accordingly, when Democrats swept the midterm elections last week, many took to social media to call for Kennedy to vacate his position.
“Unless RFK Jr. is interested in spending the next two years in front of congressional committees, he should go ahead and resign now,” Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., wrote on social media.
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., most likely the next chair of the House Judiciary Committee, has vowed to investigate Kennedy’s “wrongdoing.” Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., said on CNN that Kennedy should be one of two high-priority targets for impeachment for the House majority next year. And Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who is poised to take over the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, which has jurisdiction over Kennedy’s department, told the network he is “absolutely open” to that idea.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., who is expected next year to chair another committee with HHS jurisdiction, the Senate Finance Committee, told The Associated Press he plans to hold Kennedy and the administration accountable “for actions that have harmed children, raised health costs, and made America less healthy.”
He already launched two investigations this week into Kennedy — one into the accuracy of his testimony about a 2019 trip to Samoa and the other into his reported acceptance of hundreds of thousands of dollars in lavish gifts.
“For those that have broken the law and betrayed the trust of taxpayers and American families, nothing should be off the table,” Wyden said.
But Democrats also see MAHA followers as potential supporters
Even as many Democrats want to see Kennedy answer for his actions, others are open to working with him – and certainly with his followers.
With at least some aspects of the sprawling MAHA movement resonating with U.S. adults of both parties, such as reducing processed foods and addressing government corruption, the new Congress creates a rare opportunity for coalition building. It also helps Democrats that many MAHA followers have soured on the Republican Trump administration, seeing recent actions like an executive order boosting pesticide use as a betrayal of their trust.
More cracks in that support have emerged since the election. Calley Means, a former administration adviser and top MAHA advocate recently accused White House officials of catering to foreign and domestic lobbyists at the expense of Americans’ health. But in the interviews where he made those accusations, he also praised Kennedy.
Maine Rep. Chellie Pingree, Massachusetts Rep. Jim McGovern and New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker are among those who have teamed up with MAHA activists to devise proposals on topics like regenerative agriculture, healthy school lunches and liability for pesticide manufacturers.
Pingree told the AP she hopes that cooperation can continue, even though many of her MAHA-aligned contacts remain strong supporters of Kennedy. Whether Democratic colleagues try to impeach Kennedy is “out of my hands,” she said.
But “if he’s still there, I’m hoping we can continue to work on some of these things and make whatever gains we can.”
McGovern said he’s been clear with MAHA leaders he works with that “we need to hold RFK Jr. accountable for his broken promises and lying to his supporters while enabling the corruption he swore he would stand up to.”
“The MAHA leaders I’m talking to quietly agree and are ready to move forward together to actually fix the broken status quo in Washington,” he said.
New Democratic additions to Congress are also cautiously open to working with Kennedy and his followers. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, has called Kennedy a grifter and told the AP he wants to understand how his department made decisions over the past two years on issues like vaccine recommendations. But he said he could still collaborate with Kennedy on policies to make America healthier, on one condition.
“If he wants to be evidence driven, I’ll work with him,” El-Sayed said.
Boosting health affordability could be Democrats’ most urgent task
Democrats will also be balancing MAHA-minded legislation with goals that resonate with an even wider swath of Americans: lowering health costs and boosting healthcare access.
They plan to vote quickly to reinstate the healthcare tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, which expired in late 2025, leaving millions of Americans confronting higher health insurance costs. Proposals are also ready to reverse the Medicaid funding reductions that Republicans put in place as part of their sweeping bill of tax breaks and program cuts, including new work requirements for recipients.
Motta said Democrats’ ability to pass those kinds of changes will be one of the most important factors for keeping support among the independent and swing voters who cast ballots for them this year.
“Above all, people want the price of healthcare to go down,” he said. “The people who can do that for them are the people who will be rewarded at the ballot box.”
